paragraphs.text: Something’s Different About People Now and It’s Terrifying

paragraphs.name: e5d1
paragraphs.text: Photo by Jezael Melgoza on Unsplash

paragraphs.name: f451
paragraphs.text: Yesterday I had to rush a friend to the emergency room with a bleeding eye and a sense of doom that the world is not what it used to be and it never will be again.
I have no idea if that’s good or not for the world, but for his eye it’s bad news. For our friendship too.

paragraphs.name: af30
paragraphs.text: I’ve known him for twenty years. We were walking down the street, a normal afternoon, the kind you don’t think you’ll remember. I was talking. He was on his phone, scrolling, scrolling, scrolling.

paragraphs.name: 88bc
paragraphs.text: From time to time he would show me photos of things he thought I might like: the rare sight of an ermine on a beach in Alaska, hunting. Possibly AI. A girl going to sleep in a bed with the bedsheets made of lava. Definitely AI, I hope.

paragraphs.name: 73e9
paragraphs.text: I was telling him something — I don’t even remember what, something that mattered to me — and he was half-nodding, eyes down, thumb moving. And then, mid-sentence, a sharp tree branch caught him directly in the eye.
A proper, head first, eye-piercing collision. He walked into it the way you walk into something when you’re somewhere else entirely, which is exactly where he was.

paragraphs.name: c5ed
paragraphs.text: He was screaming. There was blood and fear and my stomach turning, and his bleeding eye throbbing. I rushed him to the emergency room.

paragraphs.name: e70c
paragraphs.text: She says we’re not addicted to our phones so much as we’re using them to avoid the discomfort of being alone with our own thoughts, and the discomfort of genuine, unpredictable human contact.

paragraph.name: eeb9
paragraph.text: He wrote about the way technology was producing a culture of self-referential noise, where everyone is broadcasting and almost nobody is receiving.

paragraph.name: cbd7
paragraph.text: His argument is that we’ve shifted from a society of discipline, where external authority told you what to do, to a society of achievement, where you internalize the pressure and become your own oppressor.

paragraph.name: 451f
paragraph.text: This is the burnout society. Term coined by Korean-German philosopher Byung-Chul Han.

paragraph.name: 5f43
paragraph.text: Just like the guy walking into you on the street without looking up. It’s not selfishness so much as a kind of social blindness — he just hasn’t registered that the street contains other people and they’re in his way. And it’s so widespread now that noticing it makes you feel like the strange one.

paragraph.name: e70c
paragraph.text: She says we’re not addicted to our phones so much as we’re using them to avoid the discomfort of being alone with our own thoughts, and the discomfort of genuine, unpredictable human contact.

paragraph.name: 6a49
paragraph.text: The terrifying part is my friend of twenty years, standing on a street in broad daylight, bleeding from his eye, and the fact that I’d already been losing him long before the branch made it visible.

paragraph.name: bb87
paragraph.text: The irony buried in all of this is almost too neat. The more we worry about artificial intelligence becoming too human, the more we seem to be becoming a little less so.

paragraph.name: b042
paragraph.text: Algorithms don’t reward nuance. They reward reaction. So the brain gets a constant feed of outrage and manufactured conflict that slowly trains it to see the world as hostile and other people as opponents.

We got comfortable with isolation. We stopped practicing the small, low-stakes interactions that keep those muscles working — the chat with the cashier, the nod to the neighbor, the accidental eye contact that becomes a smile.

paragraph.name: 49b0
paragraph.text: We’ve entered what some people are calling the age of main character syndrome, and Jonathan Franzen, this American novelist, of all people, saw something like this coming years before it had a name.
A proper, head first, eye-piercing collision. He walked into it the way you walk into something when you’re somewhere else entirely, which is exactly where he was.

paragraph.name: 6e8b
paragraph.text: Empathy takes effort and we’re tired. Community requires showing up and we’re busy. So we retreat, outsource, interact through screens, and slowly the human software starts to glitch.
